title: Curios of the week #182
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman's regular "Curios of the week" roundup for Filling the Pail opens with editorial complaint about a fellow Australian education figure, Adam Voigt, misrepresenting his views on restorative practices, then moves through a week's worth of education-world items with his own commentary attached. Its substantive core is a discussion of England's GCSE results and Daisy Christodoulou's argument that the "forgotten third" of students who miss benchmark GCSE grades in English and maths should not automatically be routed into vocational alternatives, since the students who struggle academically are not the same population suited to technical education. Ashman also uses the roundup to report his own investigative journalism into the Australian Centre for the Public Understanding of Education (ACPUE), whose leadership had been opaque until his inquiries prompted a change to its About page. A hiring notice for his own school, Clarendon, and a nod to Michaela Community School's recurring presence in GCSE results-day coverage round out the post. The retrieved copy of this email cuts off mid-sentence on the Michaela item; the remainder continues on the linked web version. It is archived here as the roundup's own editorial entry (author Ashman), reflecting his sustained commentary on GCSE assessment outcomes and education-sector accountability.
points: Opens with editorial complaint about Adam Voigt misrepresenting Ashman's views on restorative practices without correction.
Covers Daisy Christodoulou's argument that the 'forgotten third' of GCSE students need better English and maths teaching, not automatic diversion into vocational tracks.
Reports Ashman's own investigative follow-up on the previously opaque leadership of the Australian Centre for the Public Understanding of Education (ACPUE).
Includes a hiring announcement for Ashman's school, Clarendon, across multiple subjects.
Notes Michaela Community School's recurring presence in GCSE results-day news coverage, though the retrieved text cuts off before elaborating.
quotes: Roughly a third of students struggle to gain benchmark grades at GCSE and Daisy has been making the point for some time that this does not mean these students need a vocational or technical alternative.
Muddling these two groups probably accounts for much of the failure of technical and/or vocational education in England in the last few decades.

If all schools could do what some schools already appear to be doing, then it might be possible to get 80, 85 or even 90% of students over the GCSE benchmark, better preparing them for whatever they go on to in future, whether that is vocational or not.
After emailing the Australian Centre for the Public Understanding of Education (ACPUE), receiving no response and then investigating for myself, we finally have some names associated with the Centre.
Clements and Ciabatti are an interesting pair with very few published papers between them.
It's not the worst thing to ever happen, but it is deeply weird.
If someone suggests I have misrepresented them, I am usually happy to adjust a post to reflect this because it is often simply an honest error.
